name: Caesaropapism
summary: Caesaropapism is the arrangement in which the head of state is also head of the church and supreme in religious matters, so that clergy are subordinate to secular power. Britannica ties it above all to the Byzantine Empire, then to Russia from Ivan IV to Peter the Great's Holy Synod, and by extension to Henry VIII's royal supremacy. Scholars add that Byzantine texts speak of an interdependence (symphonia) of emperor and church, so the label overstates it for Byzantium. Its positions concern church and state; it has no stated programme on economics, society or foreign affairs.
scope: The tenet that the secular ruler holds supreme authority over the church, as defined by Britannica (reference) and the scholarship it summarises, with the Byzantine, Russian and English royal-supremacy cases it names. Excludes theocracy or papal supremacy (the reverse arrangement) and the wider politics of the regimes concerned, which are other subjects.

clerical-rule.rationale: The defining claim is that the secular ruler is supreme in religious matters, so churchmen holding the highest political authority contradicts it; Britannica says Peter the Great made the church a state department.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Britannica says Byzantine emperors regarded themselves as viceregents of Christ, and the scholarship says the emperor ruled by the grace of God; the sources do not state it as a doctrine about all political authority.

separate-church-state.rationale: Britannica's definition has the head of state also head of the church, and its examples (Peter the Great turning the church into a department of the state, Henry VIII) are fusions of the two, the opposite of strict separation.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Britannica defines caesaropapism as the system in which the head of state is also head of the church and supreme judge in religious matters; Peter the Great turned the Russian church into a department of the state.

missingStatements.text: The head of state should also be the head of the national church.
missingStatements.rationale: This is Britannica's definition of caesaropapism, and the scholarship describes the emperor as both political and religious leader.

notes: Themes searched: church-state relations (Byzantium, Russia, England), the ruler's sacral standing, clergy appointment. Britannica and the other sources record nothing on economy, society, liberty, world affairs, technology, ecology, means or globalism, so those are null. Britannica's Justinian article and the Byzantine scholarship dispute the label for Byzantium; answers rest on the definition and the cases where it is accepted. Peter the Great's Spiritual Regulation itself and Weber's Economy and Society were not available as open text.
